blocks.content: Puducherry's pre-colonial history centres on one especially significant archaeological site - Arikamedu - which provides some of India's best physical evidence of ancient Indo-Roman trade, making this a favourite cross-topic (history-cum-archaeology) chapter.

Arikamedu, a coastal archaeological site roughly 4-5 km south of present-day Puducherry town, has been identified by most historians and archaeologists with 'Poduke' or 'Podouke', a port mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (an ancient Greek merchant's navigational/trade guide, c. 1st century CE) as a significant trading emporium of the Tamil coast.

Excavations at Arikamedu (notably by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945 and subsequent archaeologists) uncovered substantial evidence of Indo-Roman trade, including Roman amphorae (wine/oil storage jars), Arretine ware (fine Roman pottery), Roman glass, and beads - establishing Arikamedu as one of India's most important archaeological sites documenting direct maritime trade contact between the Tamil coast and the Roman Mediterranean world in the early centuries CE.

This trade connection places ancient Puducherry within the broader story of Chola/Tamil maritime commerce along the Coromandel Coast, well before any European colonial presence - a useful point for candidates to distinguish the ancient (Roman-era) trade history from the much later (16th-18th century) European colonial history covered in Chapter 3.

★ EXAM POINT: Arikamedu is identified with 'Poduke'/'Podouke' from the ancient Greek Periplus of the Erythraean Sea - a frequently tested ancient-history fact connecting Puducherry to India's Indo-Roman trade network, entirely distinct from and predating its much later identity as a French colonial settlement.

items: The Puducherry region, like much of the Tamil coast, came under the successive overlordship of major South Indian dynasties through the medieval period, including the Pallavas (who had their capital at nearby Kanchipuram and controlled the wider Tondaimandalam region including the Puducherry coast), the Cholas (at the height of their maritime and territorial power), and later the Vijayanagara Empire and its subordinate Nayak chieftains.

By the time of the arrival of European trading powers in the 16th-17th centuries, the region was under the control of local Nayak governors owing nominal allegiance to the declining Vijayanagara Empire and, subsequently, the Sultanate of Bijapur/Golconda and Mughal-era successor polities in the wider Deccan/Tamil region, setting the stage for the European trading companies' negotiations for coastal trading rights described in Chapter 3.
Arikamedu (near Puducherry) = identified with 'Poduke'/'Podouke' from the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea; major Indo-Roman trade site (Roman amphorae, Arretine ware, glass, beads).
Excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945, among others.
Medieval overlordship: Pallavas (Kanchipuram-based) -> Cholas -> Vijayanagara Empire/Nayak governors, before European arrival.
